article.title: Six Hikers In Siberia Died Under Bizarre Circumstances In 1993 — And The Sole Survivor Couldn't Explain Why
article.description: Theories about the cause of the Khamar-Daban incident range from hypothermia to Russian nerve agents.
article.creator: Rivy Lyon
article.credit: Nguồn: Rivy Lyon · All That's Interesting
article.text:
Family of Timur BapanovIn August 1993, seven hikers ventured into the Khamar-Daban mountain range. Only one came home.

Everyone has heard of the Dyatlov Pass incident, when nine Soviet hikers perished under mysterious circumstances in the Ural Mountains in 1959. But not as many people know about the Khamar-Daban incident, an equally eerie tragedy that occurred in Russia three decades later.

On August 2, 1993, seven hikers from Kazakhstan set out for a trip through the Khamar-Daban mountain range in southern Siberia. The group was led by 41-year-old Lyudmila Korovina, an experienced hiking instructor who held a prestigious Master of Sports title. She was joined by six students between the ages of 15 and 24.

The expedition was supposed to be a challenging yet peaceful journey through the mountains. But six members of the group didn’t make it out alive.

The sole survivor was 17-year-old Valentina Utochenko, who was found wandering alone in the wilderness four days after the deaths of her fellow hikers. She described a bizarre series of events that officials struggled to explain — and much of the Khamar-Daban incident remains a mystery to this day.

The seven hikers who set out to conquer the Khamar-Daban mountain range were part of the Azimut tourist club in Petropavl, a city in northern Kazakhstan. Their leader, Lyudmila Korovina, had years of experience teaching young people how to survive difficult expeditions. Her six young students were Tatiana Filipenko, 24; Alexander Krysin, 23; Denis Shvachkin, 19; Valentina Utochenko, 17; Viktoriya Zalesova, 16; and Timur Bapanov, 15.

Family of Timur BapanovThe seven hikers as they embarked on their expedition.

The group trained together before leaving Kazakhstan, and Korovina carefully plotted their route. According to the Russian outlet Komsomolskaya Pravda, preparations began six months ahead of the trip. The schedule was planned down to the hour, and a daily food ration was allotted to each hiker.

Korovina’s team began their hike in the Buryatia region of Siberia on August 2, 1993. There were two other hiking groups in the area at the time, including one led by Korovina’s 16-year-old daughter, Natalia.

Everything initially went as planned, and the group arrived at Retranslyator Peak on August 4. But as they began to descend, a rainstorm struck. Korovina reportedly had the hikers build a camp in an exposed location, and they were unable to get a fire going due to the conditions.

Svetlana Ivanova/Wikimedia CommonsLyudmila Korovina’s group was hiking through the Khamar-Daban mountain range just below the westernmost edge of Lake Baikal.

As Utochenko told Komsomolskaya Pravda in 2018, “It was freezing cold at the summit. Early morning. We were asleep. Korovina woke us up and told us to pack our things and descend into the gorge. She was trying to save us. She just didn’t make it in time.”

The group managed to build a fire and eat breakfast together before continuing their descent. Then, tragedy struck.

While walking at an elevation of roughly 7,861 feet, Krysin — who was at the back of the group — suddenly started screaming. He fell to the ground convulsing, and foam was coming out of his mouth.

Korovina ran to Krysin, but as she reached him, she started experiencing similar symptoms. “Korovina sat down next to him, hugged him, and that was it,” Utochenko recalled. “She never got up again. And then all Hell broke loose.”

DyatlovPass.comLyudmila Korovina, the group leader who perished during the Khamar-Daban incident.

“It was like a horror movie,” Utochenko continued. “Everyone was falling; there was blood everywhere, foam coming from mouths, blood running from noses.”

Shortly after Korovina fell, Filipenko started grabbing her throat as if she couldn’t breathe. She crawled to a rock and hit her head against it repeatedly until she seemingly lost consciousness.

The two youngest hikers, Zalesova and Bapanov, then began to run, but they soon started throwing up blood and pulling off their clothes before they collapsed, too.

At this point, only Utochenko and Shvachkin remained. They also ran, but Shvachkin fell into convulsions, and Utochenko left him behind. She later said that she passed out in “a state of delirium,” and when she came to, she returned to the site of the Khamar-Daban incident to get the necessary supplies for her journey out of the wilderness.

Alava/Wikimedia CommonsValentina Utochenko was found by kayakers on the Snezhnaya River four days after her fellow hikers perished.

Utochenko wandered for four days, following power lines and rivers until she came across a group of kayakers on August 9. She tried to tell them what had happened, but she was incoherent, and she then fell into a traumatized silence.

Helicopters didn’t begin searching for the dead hikers for another two weeks, and the bodies were located on August 24. A medical examiner performed autopsies to determine what had killed the hikers — but they left more questions than answers.

According to the autopsies, five of the six hikers had died from hypothermia, while Korovina had suffered a heart attack.

The group had been in frigid conditions due to the unexpected rain, and severe hypothermia can cause victims to experience seizures and behave unexpectedly. This would explain why some of the hikers stripped off their clothing. But it would not explain why they were bleeding from the ears and nose, as Utochenko reported.

In her 2018 interview with Komsomolskaya Pravda, Utochenko gave her own opinion on the Khamar-Daban incident: “I think pulmonary edema set in. The symptoms fit — frothing, blood from the mouth, delirium.”

Public DomainThe Khamar-Daban incident has been compared to the events at Dyatlov Pass.

However, the hikers were at an elevation of less than 8,000 feet. High-altitude pulmonary edema is common in areas like Mt. Everest’s Death Zone, but it doesn’t typically appear until climbers reach elevations well above 8,000 feet.

It’s also unlikely that all six hikers would have been stricken at the exact same time. And why did 17-year-old Utochenko survive when the much more experienced members of the group and healthy men in their prime collapsed?

In the wake of the tragedy, rumors flew about its true cause — and some were more sinister than the others.

While hypothermia and pulmonary edema — or perhaps a mix of the two — remain the leading theories for the Khamar-Daban incident, several other explanations have emerged over the decades.

As rescuer Valery Tatarnikov told Komsomolskaya Pravda in 2018, “The death of Korovina’s group remains a great mystery to me. The taiga isn’t a desert or the polar ice caps. If you’re an experienced hiker — which Korovina was — and you’re in the forest in summer, it’s impossible to die of cold.”

Emilianka/Wikimedia CommonsExperts have found inconsistencies between Utochenko’s reports and the hikers’ official causes of death.

The hikers’ death certificates listed protein deficiency and malnutrition as contributing factors to their demise. While Utochenko has stated that they had plenty of food to eat, some theorists believe that Korovina was starving her students.

Another rescuer, Yuri Golius, recounted a previous encounter he’d had with Korovina. She had taken two teenage boys hiking near Lake Baikal, and when they emerged from the mountains, they were exhausted.

“I asked what was going on,” Golius told Komsomolskaya Pravda. “Korovina explained that she was practicing a sort of ‘survival school’ method — taking a group on a hike with minimal food and clothing. She claimed this was how she trained them to be ready for unforeseen situations.”

If Korovina had indeed been limiting her students’ rations, a vitamin deficiency may have made them more susceptible to hypothermia or pulmonary edema.

Other theories claim that the group ingested toxic mushrooms and roots or drank tainted water from Lake Baikal. Perhaps Utochenko didn’t consume as much as the other hikers, so her symptoms weren’t as extreme.

Opioła Jerzy/Wikimedia CommonsRescuers found golden root in the hikers’ backpacks. The plant is not toxic, but consuming too much can lower blood pressure, which could have compounded the symptoms they experienced.

Then, there’s the nerve agent theory. The Soviet Union — and later Russia — had developed a family of deadly nerve agents known as Novichok. There are claims that Russia was testing the chemical weapons in southern Siberia in the early 1990s, and the Khamar-Daban incident may have been sparked by unknown contact with the poison.

The government may have then tried to cover up the tragedy, leaving the hikers’ bodies to decompose for two weeks before trying to locate them so evidence of their complicity would go unnoticed. Corrupt officials could have even ordered the medical examiner to list hypothermia as the cause of the hikers’ deaths.

Of course, this is just one of dozens of theories about the Khamar-Daban incident. Even more than 30 years later, the tragedy remains one of the hiking world’s greatest — and eeriest — mysteries.
